claim: In 1851, Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich obtained millions of axillary temperatures from 25,000 patients in Leipzig.
source: In 1851, the German physician Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich obtained millions of axillary temperatures from 25,000 patients in Leipzig, thereby establishing the standard for normal human body temperature of 37°C or 98.6 °F (range: 36.2–37.5°C [97.2- 99.5 °F]) (Mackowiak, 1997; Wunderlich and Sequin, 1871).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mackowiak (1997) and Wunderlich and Sequin (1871), which are historical references to Wunderlich's work.

claim: Wunderlich established the standard for normal human body temperature of 37°C or 98.6°F with a range of 36.2–37.5°C (97.2-99.5°F).
source: In 1851, the German physician Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich obtained millions of axillary temperatures from 25,000 patients in Leipzig, thereby establishing the standard for normal human body temperature of 37°C or 98.6 °F (range: 36.2–37.5°C [97.2- 99.5 °F]) (Mackowiak, 1997; Wunderlich and Sequin, 1871).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to historical work by Mackowiak (1997) and Wunderlich and Sequin (1871).

claim: A compilation of 27 modern studies reported mean temperature to be uniformly lower than Wunderlich's estimate.
source: A compilation of 27 modern studies, however (Sund-Levander et al., 2002), reported mean temperature to be uniformly lower than Wunderlich's estimate.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sund-Levander et al. (2002), which compiled modern temperature studies.

claim: An analysis of more than 35,000 British patients with almost 250,000 temperature measurements found mean oral temperature to be 36.6°C.
source: Recently, an analysis of more than 35,000 British patients with almost 250,000 temperature measurements, found mean oral temperature to be 36.6°C, confirming this lower value (Obermeyer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Obermeyer et al. (2017), which analyzed a large dataset of British patients.

claim: In Wunderlich's era, life expectancy was 38 years.
source: Wunderlich obtained his measurements in an era when life expectancy was 38 years and untreated chronic infections such as tuberculosis, syphilis, and periodontitis afflicted large proportions of the population (Murray et al., 2015; Tampa et al., 2014; Richmond, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murray et al. (2015), Tampa et al. (2014), and Richmond (2014), which provide historical context about life expectancy and disease prevalence.

claim: Untreated chronic infections such as tuberculosis, syphilis, and periodontitis afflicted large proportions of the population in Wunderlich's era.
source: Wunderlich obtained his measurements in an era when life expectancy was 38 years and untreated chronic infections such as tuberculosis, syphilis, and periodontitis afflicted large proportions of the population (Murray et al., 2015; Tampa et al., 2014; Richmond, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Murray et al. (2015), Tampa et al. (2014), and Richmond (2014), which document historical disease prevalence.

claim: Human body temperature is a crude surrogate for basal metabolic rate.
source: Human body temperature is a crude surrogate for basal metabolic rate which, in turn, has been linked to both longevity (higher metabolic rate, shorter life span) and body size (lower metabolism, greater body mass).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between body temperature and metabolic rate.

claim: Basal metabolic rate has been linked to longevity, with higher metabolic rate associated with shorter life span.
source: Human body temperature is a crude surrogate for basal metabolic rate which, in turn, has been linked to both longevity (higher metabolic rate, shorter life span) and body size (lower metabolism, greater body mass).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between metabolic rate and longevity.

claim: Basal metabolic rate has been linked to body size, with lower metabolism associated with greater body mass.

evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between metabolic rate and body size.

claim: Temperature measurements were significantly higher in the UAVCW cohort than in NHANES.

claim: Temperature was directly related to weight.

claim: In STRIDE, temperature increased 0.02°C per hour of the day.

claim: In UAVCW, a rise in ambient temperature of one degree Celsius correlated with 0.001 degree (p<0.001) increase in body temperature.

claim: The use of anti-inflammatory drugs including aspirin, statins and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) increased between NHANES and STRIDE.
